historical_record.description: Built by Bethlehem Steel as the Union Iron Works hospital, to modern standards and for a far larger workforce than the house it replaced. Designed by Frederick H.
The hospital's chief physician was shot dead in the X-ray room by a shipyard worker, who then tried to kill himself.
During the influenza pandemic the hospital treated 2,594 shipyard workers, set up a temporary isolation ward, and began inoculating all 18,000 of the company's San Francisco employees.

Bethlehem closed the hospital without ceremony after the yard lost a $16 million contract for four Panama Mail Line ships, and sold the building; a succession of short-lived private hospitals followed, and from 1938 a rest home.

Henry J. Kaiser's Permanente Foundation bought the building and opened it late that year as the Permanente Harbor Hospital, the foundation's first full-service hospital in San Francisco, chosen for its nearness to the Bethlehem yard and the Hunters Point Naval Shipyard; it ran until 1958.
Kaiser Permanente sold the building, which became a 50-bed convalescent home, later the Potrero Convalescent Home and the Mission Bay Convalescent Hospital, until it closed in 2013.
The building was rehabilitated as seven apartments, its gutted interior rebuilt and its windows replaced.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places as a rare company hospital in San Francisco and as Kaiser Permanente's first full-service hospital in the city.
